findings: Anteroposterior projection of the abdomen and lower chest
Multiple curvilinear and tubular radiopaque structures distributed throughout the small bowel loops in the mid and lower abdomen, consistent with calcified or radio-opaque helminth parasites
The structures display the characteristic coiled/curved morphology of roundworm (Ascaris lumbricoides) adults
Bowel gas pattern shows moderately distended small bowel loops centrally
No pneumoperitoneum identified on this projection
Lower ribs and pelvis are partially included; iliac crests visible inferiorly
No obvious calcified renal or bladder calculi seen
Liver and spleen margins are partially obscured by overlying bowel gas
No soft tissue masses clearly delineated
differential: Ascariasis (Ascaris lumbricoides infestation): most likely given the multiple curvilinear tubular radio-opaque structures conforming to the shape and distribution of adult roundworms within small bowel
Small bowel obstruction secondary to helminth bolus: the moderate small bowel distension in conjunction with large worm burden raises concern for partial or impending mechanical obstruction
Other helminth infestation (e.g., heavy Trichuris or mixed helminthiasis): less likely given the size and coiled morphology of the opacities, but cannot be excluded without clinical correlation
anatomyConcerns: The pelvis is partially cut off inferiorly, limiting assessment of the rectosigmoid region and bladder
The upper abdomen and diaphragm are partially excluded, limiting assessment for free air under the diaphragm
Mild dextroscoliosis of the lumbar spine is a true anatomical finding rather than acquisition obliquity, as the spinous processes are rotated

imageApproval.diagnosticReason: Multiple long curvilinear tubular radiopaque structures distributed throughout the small bowel loops bilaterally, displaying the characteristic coiled and curved morphology of adult Ascaris lumbricoides worms outlined by surrounding intraluminal gas. The sheer number, size, and distribution of these opacities, combined with moderately distended small bowel loops and the clinical vignette of crampy abdominal pain and vomiting in a child, strongly supports heavy Ascaris infestation as the primary diagnosis. No equally supported alternative is identified; calcified mesenteric nodes would appear as discrete rounded calcifications rather than long curvilinear tubular structures. The mild dextroscoliosis is a true anatomical finding. The pelvis is partially included inferiorly but iliac crests are visible, slightly outside the expected crop. No pneumoperitoneum, no duplicated organs, one midline lumbar spine, bowel gas follows anatomical luminal distribution.
